precepts.text: Esau was forty years old when he took to wife Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite: which were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah. His parents did not like his marriage choices of those Hittites. Listen: you have unlearned Israelites that use these verses to say Esau was black because his kids mixed with the Hittites. No. God kept that line the way it is. Even today, no matter how black you are, if you marry a white woman you can tell that child is hybrid: high yellow, sometimes yellow hair, green eyes. Photos shown of Drake as a boy and his family: his hair is like his father, but his complexion is closer to the mother. So you mean back then God could not maintain that same lighter red complexion in Esau's line? These hybrid children look more like Esau.
precepts.point: Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright. In that pottage was meat: feed me, I pray thee, with that same red pottage, raw, bloody meat. And you have brothers today lusting after these same people. Many times brothers ask what it means that Esau was profane or a fornicator; the scriptures explain it.

note.label: We Are Born in Babylon

precepts.why:
Hebrews calls Esau a “fornicator, or profane person”, and brothers often ask what that means. The scriptures explain it, beginning with his marriages: “Esau was forty years old when he took to wife Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite: Which were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah.” His parents did not like his choice of those Hittite women.

Some unlearned Israelites use these two verses to say Esau was black, because his children were mixed with the Hittites. No. God kept that line the way it is. Even today, no matter how black you are, if you marry a white woman you can tell the child is a hybrid: high yellow, sometimes yellow hair, green eyes. Look at Drake as a boy with his family: his hair is like his father's, but his complexion is closer to his mother's.

So you mean back then God could not maintain that same look, that lighter red complexion, in Esau's line? No, God don't have that power? Shut up, Negro. Be quiet. These hybrid children look more like Esau. Mixing with the Hittites did not make Esau black; it is part of what made him a fornicator.

precepts.text: Because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws. Abraham kept the laws, statutes, and commandments just as Noah did.
precepts.point: The earth also was corrupt before God: because the sons of God started to mingle with the daughters of men, Cain's children. Cain gained dominion on the earth. And the earth was filled with violence: just like Cain was violent. Is the earth full of violence today? Yes. The end of all flesh is come before me; behold, I will destroy them with the earth.

note.label: As in the Days of Noah: Past & Present

precepts.why:
God said of Abraham, “Because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.” That is what it means to walk before God and be perfect.

Abraham kept the laws, statutes and commandments just as Noah did. “Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations, and Noah walked with God”: he kept the commandments that Seth kept, and that is why he found grace in the eyes of the Lord when the rest of the earth was corrupt and filled with violence.

So the law was not new at Sinai. Noah kept it, Abraham kept it, and those who keep it are the ones God preserves when “The end of all flesh is come before me.”

precepts.text: Because Abraham obeyed my voice and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes and my laws: past tense, what he was doing that proved his faith.
precepts.point: If thou wilt, to keep the commandments and to perform acceptable faithfulness: keeping the commandments is performing faithfulness, so your works prove your faith and your faith proves your works. That was what the last class left out for the commenters.

note.label: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Works Of The Law & Liberty

precepts.why:
God told Isaac why the promise stood: “Because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.” Abraham obeyed, and he kept the charge, the commandments, the statutes and the laws. That is past tense. It tells you what Abraham was doing from the beginning that proved his faith. His obedience was his acceptable faithfulness, the performance of Sirach 15:15.

Paul writes, “And the law is not of faith: but, The man that doeth them shall live in them.” The law meant there is the law of sacrifice, which came later. Abraham's faith came first, and his faith and the promise to him go hand in hand; the promise predates the law of sacrifice.

“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us”. The curse of the law is condemnation, not being able to atone for every sin. Caiaphas pointed it out without knowing it: “it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not.” Both the northern and southern kingdoms were under the old covenant they agreed to in Deuteronomy 27 and kept breaking, so both were condemned and destroyed by the nations. But the Lord loved them, sent his son to die for them, and took them out of that contract into a new one, “That the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ”, meaning the northern kingdom.

Paul says “before faith came, we were kept under the law”, and “the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith.” The schoolmaster is the law of sacrifice, and the “we” is Israel. After faith came, “we are no longer under a schoolmaster.” Jews, Greeks, bond, free, male and female were all the same people of God in Christ.

“And if ye be Christ’s, then are ye Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise.” Abraham is the father of faith, so his children should be children of faith like him: keeping the commandments the way he did, with faith in Christ instead of the animal sacrifice the Galatians were bewitched back into. The promise pertains to the Israelites, not to all nations.

precepts.text: The promise was to Abraham and his seed, which is Christ.
precepts.point: The reason the oath stood: because Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.

note.label: Genesis 26: The Wells and the Envy of the Philistines

precepts.why:
“In thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed.” That seed is not a crowd; it is one. “Now to Abraham and his seed were the promises made. He saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ.”

The oath sworn to Abraham and performed unto Isaac is a promise about Christ. So in thy seed shall all nations be blessed does not put everybody in the covenant. The blessing comes through Christ, and through Christ scattered Israel in all kindreds of the earth receives repentance and comes back to the Father.

precepts.text: Ye are the children of the prophets and of the covenant; unto you first God sent His Son to bless you in turning every one from his iniquities.
precepts.point: The reason the oath stood: because Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.

note.label: Genesis 26: The Wells and the Envy of the Philistines

precepts.why:
Peter says who the covenant belongs to: “Ye are the children of the prophets, and of the covenant which God made with our fathers, saying unto Abraham, And in thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed.” The children of the prophets and of the covenant are Israel, and Israel is scattered into every nation, all the kindreds of the earth.

Then how the blessing comes: “Unto you first God, having raised up his Son Jesus, sent him to bless you, in turning away every one of you from his iniquities.” The seed is Christ, and through Christ scattered Israel receives repentance, turning from iniquities and coming back to the Father. That is the blessing sworn to Abraham and performed unto Isaac; it does not put everybody in the covenant.

precepts.text: The Most High raised up prophets of the sons of Israel; the children of the prophets are Israel.
precepts.point: The reason the oath stood: because Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.

note.label: Genesis 26: The Wells and the Envy of the Philistines

precepts.why:
Who are the children of the prophets? “I raised up of your sons for prophets, and of your young men for Nazarites. Is it not even thus, O ye children of Israel? saith the Lord.” The prophets were raised up of the sons of Israel, so the children of the prophets are Israel.

That settles who Peter was speaking to when he said, ye are the children of the prophets and of the covenant. The covenant sworn to Abraham and performed unto Isaac, “in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed”, is Israel’s, scattered into every nation; it does not put everybody in it.

precepts.text: Esau's Hittite wives were a grief of mind unto Isaac and Rebekah.
precepts.point: Esau had already taken Hittite wives that were a grief of mind unto Isaac and Rebekah, and his generations show wives of the daughters of Canaan. He was hardheaded from the beginning; that is the spirit of the wicked, who hate instruction and cast the words of the Most High behind them.

note.label: Genesis 28: The Charge and the Vow at Bethel

precepts.why:
Esau had already taken wives that grieved his parents. “Esau was forty years old when he took to wife Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite: Which were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah.”

So when Esau saw “that the daughters of Canaan pleased not Isaac his father”, that was nothing new. He was hardheaded from the beginning. And instead of following Jacob’s path he went to Ishmael and took Mahalath “unto the wives which he had”: he answered his father’s grief by doing his own thing.

precepts.text: Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws; the laws are nothing new.
precepts.point: Adultery was known as sin from the beginning, long before Sinai. Abraham kept the commandments, statutes, and laws; and Abimelech rebuked Isaac because one of the people might have lain with his wife and brought guiltiness upon them. The nations themselves knew adultery brought guilt.

note.label: Genesis 39: Joseph in Potiphar's House

precepts.why:
“Because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.” Abraham kept the commandments, statutes and laws long before Sinai. The laws are nothing new.

That is how Joseph, generations before Moses, could call what Potiphar’s wife asked of him “this great wickedness” and “sin against God.” Adultery was known as sin from the beginning. Joseph knew the commandments his father’s fathers kept, and he refused.

precepts.text: Abimelech knew lightly lying with another man's wife would have brought guiltiness upon them; adultery was known sin.
precepts.point: Adultery was known as sin from the beginning, long before Sinai. Abraham kept the commandments, statutes, and laws; and Abimelech rebuked Isaac because one of the people might have lain with his wife and brought guiltiness upon them. The nations themselves knew adultery brought guilt.

note.label: Genesis 39: Joseph in Potiphar's House

precepts.why:
“And Abimelech said, What is this thou hast done unto us? one of the people might lightly have lien with thy wife, and thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us.” Abimelech rebuked Isaac because one of his people might have lain with Isaac’s wife, and that would have brought guiltiness upon them.

The nations themselves knew adultery brought guilt. If a heathen king knew it, Joseph surely knew it: lying with his master’s wife would be “this great wickedness”, and sin against God. So he refused her.

precepts.text: In the famine of Isaac's days the Lord appeared unto him and said, go not down into Egypt; the pattern of famine and Egypt runs through the fathers.
precepts.point: This is a repeating thing in our history: when famine came, the fathers moved toward Egypt for sustenance and nourishment. There was a famine in Abram's days and he went down into Egypt, and another famine in Isaac's days, when the Lord told him not to go down.

note.label: Genesis 42: Joseph's Brethren Bow Down in Egypt

precepts.why:
“And there was a famine in the land, beside the first famine that was in the days of Abraham.” In Isaac’s days the same pattern came round, and Isaac went toward Gerar; but this time “the Lord appeared unto him, and said, Go not down into Egypt; dwell in the land which I shall tell thee of.”

So the pattern of famine and Egypt runs through the fathers: Abram went down, Isaac was told not to go down, and now Jacob, seeing that there was corn in Egypt, sends his ten sons down to buy corn so the family may live and not die.

precepts.text: Because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws. This is what was going on in the tent of Abraham as long as he lived: all the laws that applied to Abraham at that time, he kept them, the sabbath day included; other laws would apply after Israel came out of Egypt.
precepts.point: That is why the Lord dealt with Abraham the way he did: Abraham was not going to choose his kids above the Most High, and they were going to do all that he commanded.

note.label: 1 Samuel 2: By Him Actions Are Weighed

precepts.why:
“Because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.” This is what was going on in the tent of Abraham as long as he lived. All the laws that applied to Abraham at that time, he kept them, the sabbath day included; other laws would apply after Israel came out of Egypt.

That is honouring the Lord, and “them that honour me I will honour.”

precepts.text: Isaac was seen sporting with Rebekah his wife, the picture of a husband playing lovingly with his own wife.
precepts.point: Be ravished always with her love, not with another woman. Married love within your own nation is what is blessed here.

note.label: Proverbs 5: The Strange Woman and Thy Labours in the House of a Stranger

precepts.why:
“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth. Let her be as the loving hind and pleasant roe; let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.” Be ravished always with her love, not with another woman.

Isaac is the picture of it: “And it came to pass, when he had been there a long time, that Abimelech king of the Philistines looked out at a window, and saw, and, behold, Isaac was sporting with Rebekah his wife.” Isaac was seen sporting with Rebekah his wife, a husband playing lovingly with his own wife.

That is the fountain that is your own and not strangers' with you. Married love within your own nation is what is blessed here.

precepts.text: Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws; that is the work of Abraham.
precepts.point: Descent from Abraham without the works of Abraham counts for nothing. The works of Abraham are believing the Most High and keeping his commandments.

note.label: Matthew 3: John the Baptist and the Baptism of the Holy Ghost and Fire

precepts.why:
What are the works of Abraham? The Most High says it plainly: “Because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.” That is the work of Abraham: believing the Most High and keeping his commandments, his statutes and his laws.

So a child of Abraham is one who does what Abraham did, obeying the voice of the Most High and keeping his commandments. Those who had Abraham to their father in the flesh but did not keep his charge could not lean on that descent. That is why John told the Pharisees and Sadducees not to think it, and why God is able of stones to raise up children unto Abraham.

precepts.text: The oath passed to Isaac's seed, "unto thee, and unto thy seed, I will give all these countries," showing the promise ran through a royal lineage, not through all nations.
precepts.point: The restitution is tied to the oath and promise, which is us being saved from our enemies and restored to our kingdom and land, because the promise was made to Abraham our father and passed through the royal seed.

note.label: Acts 3: The Restitution of All Things

precepts.why:
The oath sworn to Abraham passed to Isaac: “Sojourn in this land, and I will be with thee, and will bless thee; for unto thee, and unto thy seed, I will give all these countries, and I will perform the oath which I sware unto Abraham thy father”.

The promise ran through a royal lineage, from Abraham to Isaac to his seed, not through all nations. The countries were given to that seed, and the restitution of all things is that seed, Israel, having them restored.
